title: Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose
gist: Chatham House argues the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act 'Made in Europe' rules will force the UK to align with EU China measures: a 15 October Franco-German paper conditions UK auto access on tariffs against Chinese EVs and tighter FDI screening, ahead of the 20 November EU–UK summit. The investment demand matters more than tariffs because the UK courts Chinese car plants, and the likeliest outcome is minimal, delayed alignment that still invites Chinese retaliation (possibly rare earths or battery inputs) as Beijing seeks to make an example of the UK.

themes.theme: EU 'Made in Europe' conditionality on UK

insights.claim: The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) would condition access to certain public subsidy and procurement schemes on sufficient local European content, partly to shield European industry from cheap, high-quality Chinese goods such as hybrid and electric vehicles.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: EU industrial policy is shifting from tariffs to local-content gating of subsidies/procurement, favouring EU-footprint manufacturers over Chinese exporters.
insights.quote: The IAA plans to introduce new ‘Made in Europe’ obligations, conditioning access to certain public subsidy and procurement schemes on the use of sufficient local, European, content.

insights.claim: A 15 October 2026 Franco-German paper said 'Made in Europe' treatment for the automotive sector should be extended to the UK and a small group of other partners only on condition of reciprocity and dynamic alignment with EU rules on third-country investment and EU trade defence measures.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: UK auto access to EU schemes is explicitly priced in China-policy alignment, set by the two biggest EU car-producing states.
insights.quote: ‘dynamic alignment with EU conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defense measures’

insights.claim: In practice France and Germany want the UK to put tariffs on Chinese EVs to stop further erosion of French and German carmakers' UK market share, and to tighten FDI rules so Chinese firms cannot qualify for EU subsidies or procurement via UK-located plants.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A UK tariff on Chinese EVs would directly support European OEMs' UK share; Chinese 'back door' via UK plants is the target.
insights.locator: In practical terms, France and Germany want

insights.claim: The investment-screening demand is more consequential for the UK than the much-reported EV tariff question, because the UK wants to attract Chinese automotive manufacturing facilities to Britain.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Planned Chinese auto plants in the UK are the real casualty risk; market focus on tariffs misses the bigger investment-flow issue.
insights.quote: But the focus on investment is arguably more consequential, given the UK’s desire to attract Chinese automotive manufacturing facilities to Britain.
insights.locator: With the next EU–UK summit scheduled

insights.claim: The next EU–UK summit on 20 November 2026 is the near-term decision point forcing Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new government to address the alignment demand.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Catalyst date for UK China-trade/auto policy headlines.

themes.theme: End of UK 'cautious pragmatism' on China

insights.claim: The UK's China approach has been 'cautious pragmatism': intervening only on acute economic or security concerns, e.g. permanently high tariffs on certain steel products and blocking a proposed £1.5 billion offshore wind investment by Chinese firm Ming Yang, while courting Chinese auto investment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Precedent shows the UK will block Chinese energy-infrastructure capital but has kept autos open — that carve-out is now under pressure.

insights.claim: Despite a commitment to the US under the 2025 Economic Prosperity Deal to strengthen supply-chain security for steel and pharmaceuticals, there has so far been limited evidence of substantive UK implementation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: UK commitments to allies on China tend to be slow-walked; discount announcements until implemented.
insights.locator: However, the UK has continued to court

insights.claim: The UK relies on Chinese renewables for its decarbonization objectives, which, together with its relative size, explains its reluctance to fully align with either the EU or US approach to China.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Any China retaliation or UK restrictions could raise costs of UK net-zero buildout.
insights.locator: The UK’s reluctance to fully align

insights.claim: Because the UK cannot afford exclusion from EU procurement and subsidy schemes, the question is no longer whether it aligns with EU economic security measures but how.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Base case should be some UK alignment with EU China measures, not continued neutrality.
insights.quote: It is therefore less of a question of whether the UK will align itself with EU economic security measures than how.

themes.theme: Trade diversion of Chinese vehicles to UK

insights.claim: The EU's proposed safeguard on hybrid vehicle imports, which would restrict imports above specified quota levels, risks diverting Chinese vehicles onto the UK market, adding its own pressure on London.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect rising Chinese hybrid/EV volumes and price pressure in the UK car market if the UK stays outside EU measures — negative for incumbent European OEM UK margins.
insights.locator: But the UK can certainly not afford

themes.theme: UK policy options and their costs

insights.claim: Wholesale replication of EU measures would mean UK tariffs on Chinese EVs and a hybrid safeguard, potentially future interventions on chemicals, plastics, batteries and wind turbines, plus FDI restrictions on ownership limits, joint ventures, workforce localization and local content.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Full alignment would widen UK–China friction well beyond autos into energy-transition supply chains.

insights.claim: The UK may lack the legal tools to replicate EU measures and has historically been cautious about breaching its international obligations, making wholesale alignment hard in practice.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Implementation lag is likely even if the UK agrees politically.
insights.quote: The UK does not necessarily have the legal tools available to replicate EU measures
insights.locator: Yet this approach is not straightforward

insights.claim: A UK anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese EVs would take around a year, buying breathing space, while a safeguard investigation justified by rising Chinese imports and EU trade diversion could be quicker and, applying regardless of origin, lets the UK argue it is not singling out China.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for a UK safeguard probe as the fastest, least China-provocative route to car-import restrictions.
insights.quote: An anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese electric vehicles, for example, would take around a year to conclude

insights.claim: Brussels may care more about the political signal of UK alignment than the precise form of measures, but even so Chinese investment into UK auto manufacturing remains the hardest issue to solve without compromising wider UK economic objectives.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Symbolic trade measures may satisfy Brussels, but FDI terms are where UK growth plans collide with EU demands.
insights.locator: It also remains possible that Brussels

insights.claim: The UK could signal goodwill through new economic security tools such as a proposed anti-coercion instrument, new FDI restrictions or repackaged cybersecurity-related restrictions, but these would not automatically satisfy EU demands for alignment on specific measures.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Headline 'economic security' announcements from London may be window-dressing rather than substantive alignment.
insights.locator: The government could also seek to demonstrate

insights.claim: China would be incentivized to retaliate against UK alignment, ranging from its own tariffs on UK exports to restrictions on rare earths or battery inputs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: UK exporters and battery/EV supply chains face retaliation tail risk; rare-earth access is the key lever.

insights.claim: Beijing may have a greater incentive to make an example of the UK than to escalate with the EU, since Turkey, Morocco and Switzerland face similar EU pressure and China wants to show that aligning with EU restrictions comes at a price.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Smaller EU-adjacent economies, not the EU itself, are likelier targets of Chinese trade retaliation — a precedent-setting risk for Turkey, Morocco, Switzerland too.
insights.quote: Beijing may have a greater incentive to make an example of the UK than escalate its confrontation with the EU.
insights.locator: The UK is not the only country

insights.claim: The most likely outcome is that the UK gives the EU just enough of what it wants while delaying implementation, but Beijing will likely treat any commitment as a precedent and retaliate anyway — so the UK pays a price either way.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect a partial, delayed UK alignment deal around the summit, with Chinese retaliation risk still materialising.
insights.quote: The most likely outcome is that the UK seeks to navigate a course through these competing demands, giving the EU just enough of what it wants, while delaying implementation
